body.heading: Heavier or lighter than the sea
paragraphs: A submarine controls its depth the way a balloon controls height, but with water. To float on the surface it must weigh less than the seawater it displaces; to dive, it deliberately makes itself heavier than that water.

The adjustment happens in ballast tanks — large chambers open to the sea through vents. On the surface they hold air, keeping the boat light. To dive, the vents open, air escapes, seawater floods in, and the added weight pulls the submarine under.

body.heading: Blowing the tanks dry
paragraphs: To surface again, compressed air stored in high-pressure flasks is blown into the ballast tanks, forcing the water out. Lighter again, the submarine rises. Near the surface it can also use its engines and hydroplanes to help, but the final surfacing is buoyancy's work.

Between the extremes lies neutral buoyancy: tanks trimmed so the boat weighs exactly what it displaces, hovering at depth without rising or sinking. Keeping that balance is a constant, delicate job for the crew as fuel burns off and seawater density changes.

body.heading: Fins for the journey
paragraphs: While moving, a submarine also steers in depth with hydroplanes — small wings on the hull that tilt to push the bow up or down, like an aircraft's elevators. At zero speed they do nothing, which is why ballast, not fins, handles stopping at a depth.

The hull itself is a pressure vessel, resisting the sea's squeeze, which grows by about one atmosphere every ten metres down. Deep-diving military submarines are built to operate hundreds of metres below the surface, in permanent darkness and cold. Beyond a certain depth no pump could empty the tanks against that pressure, so surfacing from deep water is planned carefully, never improvised.

description: A submarine dives by flooding tanks until it is heavier than the water it displaces — and blows them dry to rise.
